plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

interactionPlan.concept: For a polar rose r = a·trig(nθ), the parity of n alone fixes the petal count (even n gives 2n petals, odd n gives n petals), while cosine-versus-sine only rotates the orientation and a only scales the size.

interactions.teaches: Changing n in the cosine panel reveals the parity rule in real time: even n produces 2n petals, odd n produces n petals, and the jump between these two regimes is the core of the theorem

interactions.label: n (sine panel)
interactions.teaches: Changing n in the sine panel independently confirms the same parity rule holds regardless of whether the trig function is cosine or sine — petal count depends on n's parity, not on the choice of trig function

demo_steps.title: Source default: parity contrast
demo_steps.narration: The left panel shows r = a·cos(4θ) with 8 petals (2n = 8 because n is even); the right panel shows r = a·sin(3θ) with 3 petals (n = 3 because n is odd). Side by side, the parity rule is immediately visible.

demo_steps.title: Left panel: even to odd
demo_steps.narration: Drag the left panel's n from 4 down to 3: the petal count collapses from 8 to 3, showing the dramatic jump when parity flips from even to odd.

demo_steps.title: Both odd, different functions
demo_steps.narration: Both panels now have n = 3 and both show exactly 3 petals — but their orientations differ (cosine vs sine). This confirms that the trig function controls orientation, not count.

demo_steps.title: Right panel: odd to even
demo_steps.narration: Drag the right panel's n from 3 up to 4: petals jump from 3 to 8, mirroring what happened in the left panel. The rule is universal: even → 2n, odd → n.

demo_steps.title: Amplitude only scales
demo_steps.narration: With both panels restored to the source defaults, drag the amplitude slider: all petals shrink or grow together, but the counts (8 and 3) never change.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The single number that decides how many petals a rose has is the parity of n — even n yields 2n petals and odd n yields n — and this rule holds identically for cosine and sine; the trig function only rotates the figure and a only resizes it.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side polar plots, each with its own polar grid (dotted light-gray concentric rings and 45° radial spokes), solid black axes with arrowheads, and a thick teal rose curve. Left panel caption reads 'r = a·cos(nθ), n even' in serif italic with the live numeric instance appended below (e.g. 'r = 4·cos(4θ) → 8 petals'). Right panel caption reads 'r = a·sin(nθ), n odd' with its live instance (e.g. 'r = 4·sin(3θ) → 3 petals'). Both panels are fully opaque at the default state — no ghosting or fading. The two n sliders operate independently so the panels can show different petal counts simultaneously. Petal tips should reach roughly the outer grid ring at default amplitude. Cross-fade or morph the curve smoothly when n changes.

authoredContext:
The formulas that generate the graph of a rose curve are given by r=acosnθ and r=asinnθ where a≠0. If n is even, the curve has 2n petals. If n is odd, the curve has n petals. See the figure.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

plan.concept: For a polar rose r = a·trig(nθ), the parity of n alone fixes the petal count (even n gives 2n petals, odd n gives n petals), while cosine-versus-sine only rotates the orientation and a only scales the size.
elements: polar grid: 4-5 concentric dotted gray circles centered at the origin
polar grid: dotted gray radial spokes every 45 degrees
solid black horizontal axis with arrowheads at both ends
solid black vertical axis with arrowheads at both ends
teal rose curve r = a·trig(nθ), thick stroke, all petals emanating from the origin
live equation caption beneath the plot, e.g. 'r = a·cos(nθ)' or 'r = a·sin(nθ)' with current a and n substituted
live petal-count annotation near the curve (e.g. '8 petals' / '3 petals')
panel-style label area mirroring the textbook captions 'n even → 2n petals' and 'n odd → n petals'

interactions.label: Step n
interactions.teaches: Stepping n one integer at a time makes the parity rule visible rather than memorized: at even n the rose suddenly has 2n petals, at odd n it collapses to just n petals, while each petal keeps the same angular spacing.

interactions.label: Trig function
interactions.teaches: Switching between r = a·cos(nθ) and r = a·sin(nθ) rotates the whole rose to a new orientation (cosine puts a petal on the positive x-axis, sine shifts it), but the petal count stays governed by n — separating orientation from parity.

interactions.label: Amplitude a
interactions.teaches: Dragging a stretches or shrinks every petal's maximum radius in lockstep without ever changing how many petals there are, showing that a controls size, not count.

demo_steps.title: Even n: double the petals
demo_steps.narration: With the cosine form and n = 4 the rose shows 8 identical petals — four on the axes and four on the diagonals — exactly the 2n rule for even n, matching panel (a).

demo_steps.title: Odd n: same number of petals
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the sine form and step to n = 3: now there are only 3 petals, one pointing straight down and two angled up-left and up-right, matching panel (b) and the n-petals rule for odd n.

demo_steps.title: Parity, not orientation, sets the count
demo_steps.narration: Keep the sine form but step n from 3 to 4: the orientation family is unchanged, yet the petal count jumps from 3 to 8 — proof that the jump is caused by parity alone.

demo_steps.title: Amplitude scales size, never count
demo_steps.narration: Return to cosine with n = 4 and drag the amplitude slider down: all 8 petals shrink toward the origin together while their number and spacing stay fixed, isolating a as a pure size control.

plan.keyInsight: The single number that decides how many petals a rose has is the parity of n — even n yields 2n petals and odd n yields n — whereas cosine-vs-sine merely rotates the figure and a merely resizes it.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Render one live polar plot (not two static panels): dotted light-gray concentric rings and 45-degree radial spokes, solid black horizontal and vertical axes with arrowheads on all four ends, and a thick teal rose curve drawn parametrically from the live a, n, and cos/sin settings. Below the plot show a serif-italic live caption 'r = a·cos(nθ)' or 'r = a·sin(nθ)' with the current numbers substituted, plus a small petal-count tag. On toggle, cross-fade/rotate the curve smoothly; on stepping n or dragging a, morph the petals continuously so the count change (3↔8) and the uniform size change read instantly. Keep petal tips reaching roughly the outer ring at the default amplitude so the curve fills a circular envelope like the textbook figure.
